messages.author: 37ee13540ebdcb79
messages.subject: QTL x QTL interactions
parts:
Hey everyone,

I have a question regarding the analysis of QTL x QTL interactions.
As far as I understood from the r/qtl tutorials (which are great!) we can perform QTL x QTL analyses with the scantwo-function and the multiple QTL-model for one phenotype. However, can I somehow analyse QTL x QTL interactions for identified QTL from different independent phenotypes? I have a population with five phenotypes. The phenotypes are from a bioassay that show resistance/susceptibility on a quantitative scale. They are independent replications of the same assay. (Ideally would always yield the same QTL). With my current analysis (scanone for each phenotype) I get overlapping QTL (on the same chromosome nearby the same cM) but also two QTL that show up only once in an assay. I would like to know if it is possible to include these QTL from the different phenotypes in one multiple QTL-model to see if they are somehow connected (e.g. by epistasis) to each other.

Can I include them in the formula y~Q1+Q2+Q3 for example? Or should I treat each replication as independent from each other? I hope my question is somehow understandable and I am thankful for any comment, I am worried that I am missing some important evidence for any interactions by these QTL.

Kind regards,

Thomas

messages.author: 96353e7106735838
messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] QTL x QTL interactions
parts:
You can include additional QTL in your multiple-qtl analysis; use addtoqtl() to add a QTL to a “qtl” object for the analysis.

But regarding “They are independent replications of the same assay.” I would expect that differences would not be so interesting, and would just be due to incomplete power to detect QTL and their interactions. I would focus on the average, unless I’m misunderstanfing.

karl

messages.author: 37ee13540ebdcb79
messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] QTL x QTL interactions
parts:
Thank you for your fast response!

Ok, I will try this, but perhaps it makes more sense to keep the analyses separated in this case. Maybe I can ask one more question. We also phenotyped/genotyped a second (also independent) population likewise as we did for the first population. The offspring is from the same genetic cross (exactly the same parents). Both populations were treated identically bit independently. We wanted to increase the power of our genetic analyses by adding 180 more individuals to the population with this second population.

Unfortunately, we can't compare the phenotypes directly to the first population as the absolute values differ (that means resistant/susceptible genotypes in the two populations have completely different absolute values). So I calculated relative values based on the parents which were used as references in the assays in both populations to allow for a comparison. But, would it make more sense to include an additive covariate (denoting from which population the offspring originates, e.g. Population A /B, transforming into numerical variable) to enable a merged analysis of the absolute phenotypes and their corresponding genotypes of all individuals ( > 300). As far as I understood, the additive covariate would allow differences in the average phenotype between two groups (Population A/B) but would assume an identical effect of the QTL in both groups. I hope it is somehow understandable. I am looking for the best way to do this analysis but I am still not sure, what the best approach would look like. Thanks for any suggestions!

Thomas

messages.author: 96353e7106735838
messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] QTL x QTL interactions
parts:
Imagine what you would do if this were an experiment with a simple treatment vs placebo. What would you do in that case? QTL mapping is sort of like that, where you repeat the analysis for each putative QTL position. What you might do, to handle the sort of batch effect you mention, in QTL mapping should be no different from other linear regression situations.

karl
